content: The Brown-headed Cowbird (Molothrus ater) is a small bird belonging to the icterid family. Appearance Adult Brown-headed Cowbirds have a short, finch-like bill and dark eyes. The adult male is predominantly iridescent black with a distinct brown head. In contrast, the adult female is gray, with a pale throat and fine streaking on the underparts. Breeding and Behavior This species breeds in open or semi-open areas across most of North America. It is a brood parasite, meaning it lays its eggs in the nests of other small passerine birds, particularly those that construct cup-like nests, such as the Yellow Warbler. The host parents then raise the cowbird chick, often at the expense of their own offspring. Brown-headed Cowbirds are permanent residents in the southern parts of their range, while northern populations migrate to the southern United States and Mexico. They frequently travel in flocks, sometimes mixing with Red-winged Blackbirds or European Starlings. These birds forage on the ground, often following grazing animals like horses and cows to catch insects stirred up by the larger animals. Their diet primarily consists of seeds and insects. Historically, they followed bison herds across the prairies, and their parasitic nesting behavior complemented this nomadic lifestyle. Their population expanded with the clearing of forests and the introduction of grazing animals by settlers across North America. Today, they are commonly seen at suburban bird feeders. Mafia Behavior Female Brown-headed Cowbirds can lay up to 36 eggs in a single breeding season. Over 140 different bird species have been documented raising young cowbirds. Host parents may sometimes recognize the cowbird egg and react in various ways. For example, Gray Catbirds destroy the egg by pecking it, while other species may build a new layer over the bottom of the original nest. In some cases, cowbird nestlings are expelled from the nest. However, rejecting a cowbird egg or nestling can provoke a retaliatory mafia response. According to a study by the Florida Museum of Natural History, when a parasitic egg was removed from a host nest, the cowbird returned to ransack the nest approximately 56% of the time. Additionally, cowbirds have been observed destroying nests in a behavior described as farming. This forces the host birds to construct new nests, which the cowbirds then parasitize by laying their eggs in the new nests 85% of the time.
